Plain explanation: A tariff in which the electricity price changes by time interval, often hourly or every 15 minutes, using wholesale-market prices plus supplier charges, taxes and network costs.
Why it matters: The cheapest and most expensive hours can differ materially, so timing flexible demand becomes valuable.
What EMON does: EMON reads the applicable price schedule and coordinates batteries, EV charging, heating, hot water and selected loads around user priorities.
Important limitation: A low wholesale price does not mean the total customer price is zero; taxes, fees and supplier formulas still apply.

Plain explanation: The market where electricity for each interval of the next day is traded before delivery. The resulting prices are commonly published one day in advance.
Why it matters: It gives EMON a usable planning horizon for charging, heating and load shifting.
What EMON does: EMON combines day-ahead prices with demand and renewable forecasts to prepare the next operating schedule.
Important limitation: Schedules may need revision because weather, consumption and intraday prices can change.

Plain explanation: A market that allows electricity positions to be adjusted closer to real time after the day-ahead market has closed.
Why it matters: It helps correct forecast errors and react to updated renewable production or demand.
What EMON does: Through an approved market partner, EMON can update battery or flexible-load schedules within the permitted trading window.
Important limitation: Access normally requires a supplier, trader or aggregator; households do not trade directly.

Plain explanation: The settlement price applied when actual production or consumption differs from the market position of a balance-responsible party.
Why it matters: Large deviations can create costs, while useful response can sometimes have value.
What EMON does: EMON helps market partners reduce deviation by adjusting qualified storage and loads.
Important limitation: The end-user payment method depends on the partner contract and local market rules.

Plain explanation: A tariff with predefined periods such as peak, shoulder and off-peak rather than continuously changing market prices.
Why it matters: Users can save by moving flexible demand into the lower-priced periods.
What EMON does: EMON stores the tariff calendar and schedules eligible devices accordingly.
Important limitation: The price periods may change by season, weekday or contract.

Plain explanation: A contract where the energy price is fixed for a defined period, although taxes and network charges may still change.
Why it matters: It reduces price uncertainty but usually gives less direct reward for hourly load shifting.
What EMON does: EMON can still optimise self-consumption, peak demand and device coordination under a fixed tariff.
Important limitation: A fixed tariff does not remove capacity charges, export rules or other variable components.

Plain explanation: A tariff whose price can be revised periodically by the supplier, but not necessarily every hour.
Why it matters: The bill can change over time even when the consumption pattern stays the same.
What EMON does: EMON applies the current tariff version to measured consumption and can compare eligible alternatives.
Important limitation: Contract notice periods and index formulas differ by supplier and country.

Plain explanation: A wholesale-market interval in which generators may effectively pay to place electricity on the grid because supply exceeds demand.
Why it matters: Customers on dynamic products may see very low import prices, while market-linked exporters may receive little or even pay to export.
What EMON does: EMON can charge storage, start useful loads and apply zero or limited export where supported.
Important limitation: Retail taxes, fees and contract terms mean the customer price may not become negative.

Plain explanation: The difference between the cost of buying electricity in one period and the value of avoiding or selling electricity in another.
Why it matters: Battery arbitrage is only attractive when the spread exceeds conversion losses, fees and degradation cost.
What EMON does: EMON calculates whether charging and later discharging is useful after configured constraints.
Important limitation: A large headline spread does not automatically equal profit.

Plain explanation: An estimate of future electricity prices based on available market data and modelling.
Why it matters: Forecasts help schedule flexible energy before final prices or events are known.
What EMON does: EMON distinguishes published prices from forecasts and updates the plan when new data arrives.
Important limitation: Forecasts are uncertain and should never be shown as guaranteed outcomes.

Plain explanation: Electricity taken from the public grid into a home, building or industrial site.
Why it matters: Import quantity and timing determine much of the energy bill and connection loading.
What EMON does: SYNQ measures import and EMON coordinates local generation, storage and flexible loads to reduce costly intervals.
Important limitation: Meter conventions and sign direction must be commissioned correctly.

Plain explanation: Electricity delivered from the site to the public grid, usually from solar, wind or a battery.
Why it matters: Its value depends on the export contract, market price, grid limit and local rules.
What EMON does: EMON measures export and can prioritise self-consumption, storage or controlled export.
Important limitation: Export may require registration, metering and technical approval.

Plain explanation: A control mode intended to keep net power exported to the grid at approximately 0 W.
Why it matters: It is used where export is prohibited, uneconomic or temporarily undesirable.
What EMON does: EMON uses SYNQ measurement and MOEBIUS control to reduce generation or absorb surplus with storage and loads.
Important limitation: Real systems have measurement latency and tolerances; zero export is not mathematically perfect at every millisecond.

Plain explanation: An export ceiling that changes over time according to a network, market or site condition rather than remaining fixed.
Why it matters: It can permit more renewable export when grid capacity exists and reduce export only when needed.
What EMON does: EMON applies approved limits to compatible MOEBIUS systems and records the active constraint.
Important limitation: It requires a trusted limit source and local permission.

Plain explanation: The maximum power a site is allowed to export to the grid. It may be a fixed kW value or a percentage of installed generation.
Why it matters: Without coordination, a limit can cause renewable curtailment even when flexible loads are available.
What EMON does: EMON charges FLUXX or starts approved loads before curtailing MOEBIUS output.
Important limitation: The legal limit remains authoritative even when local optimisation is possible.

Plain explanation: The deliberate reduction of available electricity generation because the grid, market or site cannot accept the full output.
Why it matters: Curtailment represents lost generation opportunity and can affect project economics.
What EMON does: EMON can reduce avoidable curtailment by coordinating storage and flexible demand.
Important limitation: Some curtailment is mandatory and cannot be avoided.

Plain explanation: A condition where part of the electricity network lacks capacity to carry all requested import or export at that time.
Why it matters: It can delay connections, trigger export limits or create flexibility opportunities.
What EMON does: EMON can respect site limits and participate in approved congestion programmes through partners.
Important limitation: Congestion products and compensation are local and not universally available.

Plain explanation: The organisation responsible for operating the local or regional electricity distribution network.
Why it matters: The DSO sets connection conditions and may procure flexibility to manage local constraints.
What EMON does: EMON can support DSO modes or limits where an authorised interface and programme exist.
Important limitation: The DSO is not usually the customer’s electricity supplier.

Plain explanation: The organisation responsible for operating the high-voltage transmission system and maintaining system-wide balance.
Why it matters: TSOs procure balancing services such as FCR, aFRR and mFRR.
What EMON does: EMON participates only through qualified market partners and eligible asset portfolios.
Important limitation: Rules, products and prequalification differ by country.

Plain explanation: The maximum import and/or export power agreed for a site connection.
Why it matters: Exceeding it can cause trips, penalties or the need for expensive reinforcement.
What EMON does: EMON monitors headroom and coordinates controllable assets against the configured limit.
Important limitation: The contracted value and physical protection settings may differ.

Plain explanation: The continuous process of keeping electricity supply and demand equal so system frequency remains stable.
Why it matters: Flexible batteries, loads and generators can help correct short-term imbalance.
What EMON does: EMON prepares and controls eligible assets according to instructions from selected market partners.
Important limitation: Participation needs qualification, telemetry, consent and a valid settlement contract.

Plain explanation: A digital portfolio that coordinates many distributed assets so they can operate as one market or grid resource.
Why it matters: Thousands of small batteries, EVs or heat pumps can create meaningful combined flexibility.
What EMON does: EMON Markets groups eligible assets while preserving each user’s limits and priorities.
Important limitation: A VPP does not mean the assets are physically connected behind one meter.

Plain explanation: A company that combines flexibility from multiple customers and represents it in electricity markets or grid programmes.
Why it matters: Most small assets need an aggregator because they cannot qualify or trade alone.
What EMON does: EMON acts as the control and user layer while selected partners provide aggregation and market access.
Important limitation: Commercial terms, fees and responsibility must be transparent.

Plain explanation: A fast automatic reserve used to stabilise grid frequency immediately after an imbalance.
Why it matters: Batteries can be well suited because they respond quickly in both directions.
What EMON does: EMON maintains qualified power headroom and follows partner instructions within battery and site limits.
Important limitation: Prequalification, response accuracy and availability requirements are strict.

Plain explanation: A balancing service activated automatically by a control signal to restore system balance after the initial frequency response.
Why it matters: It can require sustained and accurately metered changes in power.
What EMON does: EMON translates the partner setpoint into asset-level commands and records delivery.
Important limitation: The product design and settlement vary by market.

Plain explanation: A reserve activated manually or through scheduled instructions, often for longer events than FCR.
Why it matters: Industrial loads and larger batteries may be suitable when they can respond within the required notice.
What EMON does: EMON Pro manages availability, dispatch confirmation and performance evidence.
Important limitation: Production constraints and non-delivery penalties must be considered.

Plain explanation: A deliberate change in electricity consumption in response to price, grid or market signals.
Why it matters: Demand can provide flexibility without building additional generation.
What EMON does: EMON controls only pre-approved loads within comfort, process and safety constraints.
Important limitation: Demand response is not uncontrolled shutdown; the operating envelope must be defined.

Plain explanation: A mechanism that pays qualified resources for being available to support adequacy during future system stress.
Why it matters: Flexible demand and storage may earn availability revenue in some countries.
What EMON does: EMON can provide monitoring and control needed by a selected partner.
Important limitation: Capacity markets do not exist in the same form everywhere.

Plain explanation: A defined period when an asset is requested to increase, reduce or shift power.
Why it matters: Clear event records are needed to prove delivery and calculate settlement.
What EMON does: EMON shows the request, user constraints, delivered response and event result.
Important limitation: An event can be cancelled or excluded when safety or user priorities require it.

Plain explanation: An estimate of what a site would have consumed or produced if a flexibility event had not occurred.
Why it matters: Market settlement often compares actual performance with this reference.
What EMON does: EMON stores interval data and applies the approved partner baseline method.
Important limitation: Baselines can be disputed if the method does not reflect normal operation.

Plain explanation: The estimated percentage of usable energy currently stored in a battery.
Why it matters: SOC determines how much the battery can charge, discharge or reserve for backup.
What EMON does: EMON uses SOC together with power limits, forecast and user priorities.
Important limitation: SOC is an estimate from the battery management system, not a direct fuel gauge.

Plain explanation: An estimate of how the battery’s present capacity or performance compares with its condition when new.
Why it matters: SOH helps evaluate ageing, warranty and available flexibility.
What EMON does: EMON displays supported health information and keeps it in the service history.
Important limitation: Different manufacturers calculate SOH differently.

Plain explanation: The rate at which energy is entering the battery, normally expressed in kW.
Why it matters: It determines how quickly the battery can absorb solar surplus or low-price energy.
What EMON does: EMON respects battery, inverter, connection and temperature limits when scheduling charge.
Important limitation: Power is not the same as stored energy; 5 kW for one hour equals about 5 kWh before losses.

Plain explanation: The rate at which the battery supplies electricity to the site or grid.
Why it matters: It limits how much peak demand the battery can cover at one moment.
What EMON does: EMON allocates discharge power among peak shaving, household demand, backup and market commitments.
Important limitation: The maximum may vary with SOC, temperature and battery configuration.

Plain explanation: The amount of stored energy available for normal operation after protected top and bottom limits.
Why it matters: A 10 kWh nameplate battery may provide less than 10 kWh usable energy.
What EMON does: EMON schedules only the capacity reported as usable and preserves configured reserve.
Important limitation: Capacity can decline with age and operating conditions.

Plain explanation: The percentage of charged energy that can later be recovered after battery and conversion losses.
Why it matters: It reduces the value of tariff arbitrage and must be included in calculations.
What EMON does: EMON evaluates the price spread after configured efficiency assumptions.
Important limitation: Efficiency changes with power, temperature and equipment.

Plain explanation: The portion of battery capacity kept available for an outage or other priority use.
Why it matters: A larger reserve improves resilience but leaves less capacity for daily optimisation.
What EMON does: EMON can adjust reserve by user mode, weather, outage risk and next-day forecast where supported.
Important limitation: Backup operation also requires compatible inverter and electrical design.

Plain explanation: Charging when electricity is cheaper and discharging when it avoids a more expensive purchase or earns higher value.
Why it matters: It can reduce cost under dynamic or time-of-use tariffs.
What EMON does: EMON compares spread, efficiency, reserve and battery limits before scheduling.
Important limitation: Gross spread is not net profit; fees and degradation matter.

Plain explanation: A measure of battery use equivalent to charging and discharging its full usable capacity once, even if completed through several partial movements.
Why it matters: Cycle count influences ageing and warranty conditions.
What EMON does: EMON tracks supported energy throughput and avoids unnecessary cycling when value is weak.
Important limitation: Not all cycles have equal impact; depth, power and temperature matter.

Plain explanation: A way to express charge or discharge power relative to battery capacity. A 1C rate would charge or discharge the nominal capacity in about one hour.
Why it matters: It helps compare batteries of different sizes and understand power capability.
What EMON does: EMON stays within the limits supplied by FLUXX and the inverter.
Important limitation: Actual available C-rate can change with SOC and temperature.

Plain explanation: The share of locally generated solar electricity used on site instead of exported.
Why it matters: Higher self-consumption can increase value when avoided import is worth more than export.
What EMON does: EMON coordinates FLUXX, XOOM, OGO and OZZY loads around verified solar surplus.
Important limitation: Maximising self-consumption is not always cheapest under every tariff.

Plain explanation: The share of total site consumption supplied by local generation and storage over a period.
Why it matters: It indicates dependence on grid imports.
What EMON does: EMON reports self-sufficiency separately from self-consumption.
Important limitation: A high annual percentage does not guarantee backup during an outage.

Plain explanation: An estimate of future PV output based on system data, weather and sun position.
Why it matters: It helps reserve battery capacity and schedule flexible demand.
What EMON does: EMON updates the plan when the forecast changes.
Important limitation: Cloud cover and local shading create uncertainty.

Plain explanation: An estimate of future wind generation using weather and turbine characteristics.
Why it matters: Wind can vary quickly and affects storage and market schedules.
What EMON does: EMON combines PROP or supported wind data with demand and tariff forecasts.
Important limitation: Local terrain and turbine availability affect accuracy.

Plain explanation: The loss that occurs when available DC solar power exceeds the inverter’s maximum AC output.
Why it matters: Some clipping can be an intentional design trade-off, but persistent clipping may indicate lost yield.
What EMON does: EMON shows inverter power limits and production context where measured.
Important limitation: Not every flat production curve is clipping; export limits or grid voltage may also cause reduction.

Plain explanation: The inverter function that continuously searches for the voltage and current at which a PV string produces maximum power.
Why it matters: Correct string allocation affects performance and diagnostics.
What EMON does: EMON records which panels and strings are assigned to each MOEBIUS MPPT.
Important limitation: MPPT control remains inside the inverter; EMON documents and monitors it.

Plain explanation: The documented relationship between solar modules, their series string and the inverter input.
Why it matters: It makes commissioning, fault finding and future replacement faster.
What EMON does: EMON links ANDO serials and roof positions to the MOEBIUS MPPT record.
Important limitation: The map is only reliable if the installer scans and assigns components correctly.

Plain explanation: The ratio between electrical energy entering and leaving the inverter after conversion losses.
Why it matters: It affects delivered energy and heat generation.
What EMON does: EMON reports supported inverter power and energy data and can flag unusual performance.
Important limitation: Efficiency varies with load, voltage and temperature.

Plain explanation: Additional energy produced by the rear side of a bifacial module from reflected and diffuse light.
Why it matters: It depends strongly on mounting height, ground reflectance, spacing and shading.
What EMON does: EMON can record module type and project configuration and compare measured system output.
Important limitation: Do not apply one universal gain percentage to every project.

Plain explanation: The use of storage or flexible demand to consume renewable energy that would otherwise be limited.
Why it matters: Recovered energy can reduce imports or create productive load.
What EMON does: EMON detects approaching export limits and activates approved flexibility before curtailment.
Important limitation: The available load may be smaller than the surplus, so some curtailment can remain.

Plain explanation: Moving electricity consumption from one time period to another without eliminating the underlying service.
Why it matters: It can reduce cost, avoid peaks and use more renewable energy.
What EMON does: EMON schedules batteries, EVs, heating, hot water and selected processes inside user constraints.
Important limitation: Some loads cannot be shifted and should be classified as fixed or critical.

Plain explanation: Reducing the highest import demand by using storage or temporarily reducing flexible loads.
Why it matters: It can lower demand charges, avoid capacity penalties and protect the connection.
What EMON does: EMON monitors headroom and coordinates FLUXX and controllable loads.
Important limitation: Peak shaving does not necessarily reduce total energy consumption.

Plain explanation: The highest average power measured during a defined interval, such as 15 or 30 minutes.
Why it matters: Many commercial tariffs charge partly according to this value.
What EMON does: EMON forecasts and displays the interval peak and acts before the interval closes where possible.
Important limitation: The measurement interval and billing rule differ by tariff.

Plain explanation: A network or supplier charge based partly on the highest or contracted power rather than only kWh consumed.
Why it matters: Short simultaneous loads can therefore affect the bill for a month or year.
What EMON does: EMON coordinates EV, heating, batteries and other loads against the relevant threshold.
Important limitation: Capacity tariff formulas differ significantly by country and customer class.

Plain explanation: A rule defining which devices or processes should continue first when power is limited.
Why it matters: It prevents optimisation from interrupting safety, comfort or production-critical functions.
What EMON does: EMON lets homeowners use simple modes and professionals define detailed priority levels.
Important limitation: Priority design must be reviewed when site use changes.

Plain explanation: A device or process whose timing or power can change within defined limits without unacceptable impact.
Why it matters: Flexible loads are the foundation of cost optimisation and demand response.
What EMON does: EMON records availability windows, minimum run time, deadlines and comfort or process limits.
Important limitation: Flexibility is conditional, not permanent.

Plain explanation: A load that must remain supplied or cannot be interrupted without safety, operational or serious comfort consequences.
Why it matters: Critical loads must override commercial optimisation.
What EMON does: EMON excludes them from normal shedding and can reserve backup capacity where supported.
Important limitation: Critical classification requires competent site design.

Plain explanation: A device or circuit that EMON can start, stop or modulate through an approved interface.
Why it matters: Control enables automation rather than monitoring alone.
What EMON does: EMON uses OZZY, XOOM, NENDO and other supported controls according to permissions.
Important limitation: A measurable load is not automatically controllable.

Plain explanation: Electricity used by equipment that is not delivering its primary service but remains energised.
Why it matters: Small continuous loads can become meaningful over a year.
What EMON does: EMON identifies repeated baseload patterns and controls suitable OZZY-connected devices.
Important limitation: Some standby functions are required for safety, updates or remote access.

Plain explanation: The temporary reduction or disconnection of selected loads to keep the system within a power or reliability limit.
Why it matters: It can prevent a main fuse trip or preserve critical operation.
What EMON does: EMON follows a configured priority sequence and records the action.
Important limitation: It should not be used on unsafe or process-critical equipment without engineering approval.

Plain explanation: Charging that changes start time or power according to departure need, tariff, solar and site limits.
Why it matters: An EV is often connected much longer than it needs to charge, creating flexibility.
What EMON does: EMON controls XOOM within the user’s required energy and departure deadline.
Important limitation: Vehicle, charger and connection limits still apply.

Plain explanation: Charging an EV using available on-site solar generation, often by varying charging power with surplus.
Why it matters: It can increase self-consumption and reduce grid purchases.
What EMON does: EMON uses SYNQ surplus measurement and XOOM control, with minimum-current logic.
Important limitation: Low or variable solar may not meet the charger’s minimum stable power.

Plain explanation: A required battery level or energy amount by a chosen departure time.
Why it matters: It lets EMON optimise timing without risking an undercharged vehicle.
What EMON does: EMON calculates the latest safe charging window and preserves grid and site constraints.
Important limitation: The target depends on vehicle data or user input.

Plain explanation: The electrical current allocated to an EV charger, which determines charging power together with voltage and phase count.
Why it matters: Dynamic current control allows several chargers to share a limited connection.
What EMON does: EMON adjusts XOOM current within standards and configured limits.
Important limitation: Rapid changes and minimum current depend on vehicle and charger behaviour.

Plain explanation: Heating a building or thermal store before the period when heat is needed or electricity becomes expensive.
Why it matters: The building or tank can store useful heat for a limited time.
What EMON does: EMON uses temperature limits, forecast and tariff to schedule NENDO or OGO.
Important limitation: Excessive preheating wastes energy and reduces comfort.

Plain explanation: Cooling a building, cold room or process before a high-price or high-load period.
Why it matters: Thermal inertia can reduce later compressor demand.
What EMON does: EMON respects temperature and product limits while scheduling cooling.
Important limitation: Humidity, product quality and comfort must remain controlled.

Plain explanation: The storage of useful heating or cooling in water, building mass, ice or another medium.
Why it matters: It can shift electricity use without an electrochemical battery.
What EMON does: EMON coordinates thermal charge and discharge through supported heating or cooling equipment.
Important limitation: Thermal energy is not directly interchangeable with electrical energy.

Plain explanation: Coefficient of performance: the heat delivered divided by electricity consumed under specified conditions.
Why it matters: A COP of 4 means roughly four units of heat for one unit of electricity at that moment.
What EMON does: EMON can use operating data and temperature context where available.
Important limitation: COP changes with source temperature, flow temperature, defrost and part load.

Plain explanation: Planning when a water heater or heat-pump boiler raises tank temperature.
Why it matters: The tank provides flexibility because hot water can be prepared before use.
What EMON does: EMON schedules OGO around solar, tariff, hygiene and user demand.
Important limitation: The tank must still reach required hygiene temperatures.

Plain explanation: A periodic high-temperature hot-water cycle intended to reduce Legionella risk in relevant systems.
Why it matters: Energy optimisation must never prevent required hygiene operation.
What EMON does: EMON treats the configured hygiene cycle as a mandatory constraint and can schedule it in a favourable window.
Important limitation: Requirements depend on system design and local guidance; professional configuration is needed.

Plain explanation: A customer data port used by smart meters in several European markets to provide near-real-time electricity and sometimes gas data.
Why it matters: It can give EMON an economical verified measurement foundation.
What EMON does: SYNQ P1 reads supported telegrams and supplies import, export and tariff data to EMON.
Important limitation: P1 availability, activation and protocol version differ by country and meter.

Plain explanation: An electricity meter compliant with the EU Measuring Instruments Directive for specified legal metrology uses.
Why it matters: MID status can matter when measurements support billing or formal allocation.
What EMON does: EMON records the SYNQ meter identity and uses its interval data.
Important limitation: MID compliance alone does not authorise every billing arrangement.

Plain explanation: A sensor placed around a conductor to measure current without routing the full load through the meter electronics.
Why it matters: CT direction and ratio must be correct for accurate import, export and phase data.
What EMON does: EMON commissioning guides the installer through CT mapping and direction checks.
Important limitation: Incorrect orientation can reverse the sign or distort measurements.

Plain explanation: A widely used industrial communication protocol that exchanges data through defined registers over serial or Ethernet networks.
Why it matters: It connects meters, inverters and equipment in professional energy systems.
What EMON does: EMON uses supported register maps and records the integration status.
Important limitation: Two devices can both support Modbus but still require different register definitions.

Plain explanation: The Open Charge Point Protocol used for communication between EV chargers and management platforms.
Why it matters: It enables remote status, control, sessions and configuration for compatible chargers.
What EMON does: EMON uses supported OCPP functions for XOOM or approved project integrations.
Important limitation: Supported OCPP version and optional functions must be verified.

Plain explanation: A software interface that allows systems to exchange data or commands through defined requests.
Why it matters: Cloud APIs can connect tariffs, weather, suppliers and selected equipment.
What EMON does: EMON authenticates to approved APIs and labels the data source and availability.
Important limitation: Cloud APIs can change, fail or impose rate limits.

Plain explanation: The delay between a measured event, a decision and the resulting device response.
Why it matters: High latency can weaken zero-export, balancing or safety-adjacent control.
What EMON does: EMON chooses local or cloud control paths according to the function and supported hardware.
Important limitation: Cloud-dependent functions cannot guarantee instant response during network disruption.

Plain explanation: The time interval or granularity of recorded energy data, such as one second, one minute or 15 minutes.
Why it matters: Fine data reveals fast peaks; coarse data is easier to store and matches some billing intervals.
What EMON does: EMON uses the appropriate resolution for live control, reports and market evidence.
Important limitation: Higher resolution does not automatically mean higher accuracy.

Plain explanation: The configured sign convention that distinguishes import from export and consumption from generation.
Why it matters: A reversed meter or CT can make the entire system model incorrect.
What EMON does: EMON commissioning runs direction checks using known load or generation conditions.
Important limitation: The test must be performed safely by the installer.

Plain explanation: The assignment of measured circuits, CTs and devices to the correct electrical phase.
Why it matters: Correct mapping is needed for phase limits, diagnostics and three-phase balancing.
What EMON does: EMON records phase relationships and flags inconsistent readings.
Important limitation: Physical wiring changes require the map to be updated.

Plain explanation: Using a printed QR code to identify a product, serial number or project and open the correct commissioning flow.
Why it matters: It reduces typing errors and links the physical device to its digital record.
What EMON does: EMON scans STROHM QR codes and pre-fills supported product data.
Important limitation: A damaged or replaced label may require manual verification.

Plain explanation: Using near-field communication by tapping a phone near a product tag to identify or configure it.
Why it matters: It offers a fast local interaction without manually entering identifiers.
What EMON does: EMON opens the relevant product record and supported setup steps.
Important limitation: Phone compatibility and tag placement must be considered.

Plain explanation: A method where compatible devices help create or extend a local wireless network and discover one another.
Why it matters: It can reduce repeated network setup across a multi-device STROHM system.
What EMON does: EMON guides discovery and shows which products joined successfully.
Important limitation: Radio conditions, walls and local interference still affect reliability.

Plain explanation: The process of finding compatible devices on a local connection without entering each address manually.
Why it matters: It speeds installation and reduces configuration mistakes.
What EMON does: EMON lists detected devices and asks the installer to confirm identity and role.
Important limitation: Discovery does not replace electrical verification.

Plain explanation: Linking each product serial number to its exact project role, location or circuit.
Why it matters: It creates traceability for warranty, service and replacement.
What EMON does: EMON stores serials for panels, inverters, batteries, meters and other STROHM products.
Important limitation: Scanning the wrong physical position creates a misleading record.

Plain explanation: The structured verification that installed equipment is correctly connected, configured, tested and ready for operation.
Why it matters: Commissioning turns installed hardware into a verified system.
What EMON does: EMON guides product-specific checks and records evidence, settings and results.
Important limitation: EMON does not replace legally required tests or competent-person responsibility.

Plain explanation: A permanent structured record of product identity, mappings, settings, photos, warranties, service and ownership permissions.
Why it matters: It reduces lost documentation and supports the full system life.
What EMON does: EMON creates a passport for every commissioned STROHM system.
Important limitation: Access must follow user permissions and privacy rules.

Plain explanation: The version of embedded software running inside a device.
Why it matters: Firmware can affect compatibility, features, cybersecurity and fault behaviour.
What EMON does: EMON records supported versions and can highlight a fleet-wide issue.
Important limitation: Updates must follow vendor instructions and should not be applied blindly.

Plain explanation: The inverter configuration that applies the technical requirements of the relevant grid connection standard or country profile.
Why it matters: Incorrect settings can cause unsafe or non-compliant operation.
What EMON does: EMON records the selected MOEBIUS profile and commissioning evidence.
Important limitation: Only authorised settings and competent installers should change it.

Plain explanation: A recorded outcome for each required check, including evidence or a reason when a check cannot pass.
Why it matters: It makes incomplete work visible before handover.
What EMON does: EMON prevents silent omission and generates the final report from validated results.
Important limitation: A software pass does not override statutory inspection requirements.

Plain explanation: The estimated reduction in energy cost before subtracting subscriptions, equipment cost, finance, maintenance or tax effects.
Why it matters: It is useful for understanding the operating opportunity but is not the final financial result.
What EMON does: EMON reports the measured or modelled energy component separately.
Important limitation: Do not present gross saving as net profit.

Plain explanation: The remaining financial benefit after relevant operating costs and fees are deducted.
Why it matters: It gives a more honest view of customer value.
What EMON does: EMON can show subscription and partner fees alongside measured energy effects where data is available.
Important limitation: Capital cost and financing may still be outside the app result.

Plain explanation: A cost that did not occur because EMON changed operation, such as avoided peak import, negative export or a deferred upgrade.
Why it matters: Avoided cost is often as important as direct revenue.
What EMON does: EMON records the operational action and calculation basis.
Important limitation: A deferred investment is not the same as cash received.

Plain explanation: Payment received for making verified flexible power or energy available or delivering it during an event.
Why it matters: It can add value to batteries, EVs, heat pumps and industrial loads.
What EMON does: EMON Markets shows qualified events and partner settlement where available.
Important limitation: Revenue is not guaranteed and can vary materially by market.

Plain explanation: The calculation and payment process after energy trading or a flexibility event, including delivered volume, prices, fees and exclusions.
Why it matters: Transparent settlement is necessary for user trust.
What EMON does: EMON displays the data supplied by the selected market partner in a clear event record.
Important limitation: Final settlement authority remains with the contracted partner.

Plain explanation: A maximum monthly charge applied to a defined group of EMON modules even when their individual prices would add to more.
Why it matters: It keeps multi-device optimisation commercially predictable.
What EMON does: EMON shows selected modules, the uncapped subtotal and the applicable cap.
Important limitation: Premium services outside the cap must be labelled separately.

Plain explanation: The time required for cumulative financial benefit to equal the initial investment.
Why it matters: It is a simple comparison measure for energy projects.
What EMON does: EMON or a linked calculator can use measured load and transparent assumptions.
Important limitation: Payback ignores benefits after the payback date and may ignore financing or discount rate.

Plain explanation: A warning that projected ROI depends on future prices, behaviour, weather, equipment performance and regulation.
Why it matters: It prevents illustrative examples from being mistaken for guarantees.
What EMON does: EMON labels assumptions, country availability and whether results are measured or modelled.
Important limitation: Financial decisions may require professional advice.

Plain explanation: A clear status such as Available now, Partner required, Project-based, Coming later or Not available.
Why it matters: A pan-European website must not imply identical services in every market.
What EMON does: EMON shows availability by country, hardware and partner.
Important limitation: Labels require an owner and review date to remain reliable.

Plain explanation: The user’s explicit authorisation for data access, control, market participation or sharing with an installer or partner.
Why it matters: Energy data can reveal occupancy and operating patterns, while control can affect equipment.
What EMON does: EMON uses role-based permissions, audit trails and separate consent for optional uses such as marketing photos.
Important limitation: Consent must be specific, revocable where applicable and aligned with law.
